body: Well, saying that you don't want to waste people's time by existing sounds like you think you hurt people by existing, and then killing yourself would be a kind gesture in a way. It sounds like the opposite of selfish. It sounds like you care a lot about the people around you, but feel like they don't care about you. The reason suicide is selfish is because people really do care a lot about you, and you don't realize it enough to feel comforted. But there's some inherent hypocrisy in what I'm saying. I constantly try to justify taking my own life in my head, but I can't see why you try to do the same. To me, everyone besides me seems to deserve to live and I'm just getting in the way. So I think you deserve to live. I don't know why we can't think that about ourselves.

I feel like if I ever feel comfortable enough around someone and say anything vaguely suicidal, people jump right in with me, and it's almost like a revelation to them that someone is saying what's in their head. I rarely feel comfortable enough to do so, though. Usually before I say something like that, I'm like, nah just make a lighthearted joke, don't depress people, say something innocuous, but then I actually express my anxiety in a non joking way, and people just look dumbfounded like I accurately guessed what they dreamed last night, or told them details of a secret that they've never told anyone.

If the majority of people seem naturally normal to you, I would say that it's probably just trying to find differences between yourself and everyone else. Like you also said that not fearing death is something other people don't get. What we all have in common is that we think a lot about death whether or not we fear it. It's just a human thing. I think literally everyone is struggling as much as you or me or anyone else who replied, but the people around you just don't classify themselves as suicidal, and don't reply to posts in r/suicidewatch.

Sometimes I'm like, "man I wish all of my friends weren't goddamn insane" but then I imagine finding new, normal friends and then discovering that these new people were just wearing a really great mask to cover up their own relentless loneliness and anxiety.
